ADHD, autism or complex trauma? [pdf] > being stronger tends to sound better, even if it has other trade-offs, you know? That feels like a tautology. From context, you've defined stronger to mean better. So of course in that case stronger is better. But in  reality  stronger isn't always better. If you come to a chess match being able to bench more than your opponent, are you better at chess than them? If there are tradeoffs, and there are always tradeoffs, then you can't actually say stronger is better. The neglect of your parents might make you more independent and you might find that helps with your work life, while at the same time it makes your personal relationships harder. Which of those do you happen to value more? Which is not to say you can't personally find value in and appreciate even the negative the experiences that made you who you are. But you can't say something like: neglect is good because it makes people stronger. It could be true for your life and what you value, but it's not objectively true.

With most information hidden, the game Stratego had stumped AI until now None of the pros are doing useless APM outside of maybe early-game hand-warmups (before there's anything to do, a lot of clicking is just to keep the hands warm and ready). Indeed, pros regularly go from 300apm average to like 800apm during critical fights, but only for a minute (maximum). Humans _can_ go well above the 300apm average and do so. (Indeed, keeping your hands warm and performing "useless" 300apm in the early game is critical to keeping the blood flowing and your fingers ready for the middle game). Nonetheless, the ghost micro that Pluto demonstrated is demonstrably superhuman. No one clicks that fast or precisely with the mouse. --------------- Indeed: the only way humans reach 300apm consistently is because of _keyboard_ shotcuts. Tapping buttons on a keyboard (which don't move and are always consistent) still counts as an "action". A "mouse action", which requires you to move the cursor, and then click accurately on a moving unit, is far more intensive than clicking "55" to recenter your map upon your starting Hatchery (assuming classic handstance: Zerg often put the starting hatchery on 5 and their middle or index-finger on the 5 so that their pinky can reach s and d, for "select larvae" then "drone"). The keyboard shortcut of "55sd" is 3 actions, but far easier to perform than the 3 actions of "select ghost -> lockdown -> target". --------- I believe Slayer Boxer's famous ghost micro was accomplished with hotkeys 1234567890, so he could set off 10 lockdowns with 1l-click 2l-click 3l-click 4l-click 5l-click 6l-click 7l-click 8l-click 9l-click 0l-click. And that was a long time ago: it probably was a SlayerBoxer exhibition match (ie: he agreed with the opponent to go ghosts and the opponent to go battlecruisers before the match started, so that it was more of a crowd entertainment game rather than a serious tournament). This is the human limit of ghost micro, 10 precise lockdowns into a nuke. And only if _EVERYTHING_ was lined up for it and the opponent is even (mildly) working with you to try to make the most entertaining game. What Pluto is doing is so far outside of normal... that its nearly useless for us to study. I dunno, maybe some deeper analysts will look at some other tidbits of Pluto's build orders but I personally think its APM feats / clicking feats are just too far outside of human that there's no way anything else is worth studying. I think there's an argument that Pluto's TvT game is at least somewhat realistic and maybe humans can learn from it. But the jury is still out, people are still trying to analyze these games and understand the techniques, strategies, and tactics.

What is going on with ceiling fans Your local inspector may have opinions about this, but you can buy all the components of an excellent LED system from your favorite electronics distributor, e.g. DigiKey. Don’t waste your time or eyeballs with “driverless” devices. Get a chip-on-board LED, e.g. Bridgelux’s products, along with a matching driver (I like Luminus Devices’ small drivers - they have good startup and dimming behavior). Aside from usual electrical safety, anyone designing what is effectively a luminaire needs to make sure that the driver matches the LED and that the driver is compatible with the dimmer in use. Matching the LED means that the driver produces an amount of current that that LED’s datasheet data is acceptable and that produces the amount of light that is desired and dissipates an amount of heat that can be managed.  And that the LED’s voltage drop at the design current is in range for the driver.  These LEDs are constant  current  devices, so you’re thinking about current first and voltage second. Read the datasheets! Unfortunately many cheap luminaires are based on modules that are either driverless LEDs (which are  terrible  due to essentially unavoidable flicker and lack of regulation) or are line-voltage-supplied integrated devices.  These are likely to be hard-to-find modules.  There may not be room for a discrete driver and separate LED.

Good teams and coaches go for the Super Bowl every year because it is impossible to predict when you’ll get there and win. That includes when you have (or don’t have) a great quarterback. You just have to try your hardest every year and hope. And excellence is a habit, not a dial you can quickly turn from one side to the other over the summer. Most players have short careers and so a team needs them to get better every year in order to hope to peak as a team. It seems to me like a lot of sports criticism is based in regretful retrospection. “Oh, if only they’d done this or that, they would have won.” But it’s impossible to know what would have happened. Injuries alone are unpredictable and hugely impactful from year to year. It’s a natural thought, but that doesn’t mean it’s a good way to actually manage a team.
